items.title: Waller puts 50bp in writing hours before CPI — and MOVE is at 86
items.idea: A voting governor said a 50bp December hike 'should be considered' if core prints ~0.3% again, that hiking only 25 'puts credibility at risk', and that policy 'has not been nearly as restrictive as I thought' (take back the three insurance cuts). MOVE fell 7.3% Monday to 85.98, the calm end of its range. Dauber: 'asymmetry sits on the hot side and rate vol is priced for the cool one.'
items.angle: Cheap convexity question: if rate vol is at the floor into a print with a written 50bp tail, what's the cheapest way to own it (payer swaptions, front-end put spreads)?
items.tweetA: MOVE at 86 on the morning a voting governor wrote '50bp' in a speech. Either the options market knows something Waller doesn't, or nobody priced the tail. I know which side I'd rather be long.
items.tweetB: Everyone's trading the second decimal of core CPI. Nobody is asking why the rates vol surface treats a 50bp hike like a 0% probability event. Tails don't announce themselves in advance - Waller just did.

items.title: No YoY CPI today: 1y swap <2.0% vs households at 3.9% - same horizon, 2-point gap
items.idea: The BLS publishes no year-on-year CPI for October (Oct 2025 was never collected in the shutdown). 1-year headline inflation swap trades under 2.0%, lowest since spring, while the NY Fed survey has households at 3.9% one-year. Dauber notes a 0.3% headline vs September's 0.6% will read 'cooling' on every screen at 8:31 even though estimates run ~4.0% headline / 2.7-2.8% core YoY.
items.angle: Headline-risk setup: monthly print will be framed as disinflation while YoY (not published) sits near 4%. Fed reaction function is anchored to the thing nobody will see.
items.tweetA: The market's 1y inflation swap says <2%. Households say 3.9%. Same year, same prices, 190bp apart - and only one of them is buying groceries. Today's CPI will tell you which one is wrong.
items.tweetB: A CPI release with no year-over-year number is a Rorschach test. 0.3% headline 'cooling' from 0.6% - while the annual rate is ~4%. Expect every screen to say disinflation at 8:31 and the Fed to ignore it.

items.title: The 2-year rose 5bp the day Brent fell 6% - front end is trading Waller, not oil
items.idea: Dauber's thesis (65/35): Monday's 2y move against the barrel shows the front end is pricing the reaction function, not energy. Counter-case (Robin Brooks): Fed's year was driven by the yield curve and irritation at the President, inflation 'barely matters'; hawks 'morph back into doves'. Tells: 2y vs 4.65% (9bp away), 10y vs 4.80/5.05%, today's $39B 10y auction. Global net count of CBs cutting has rolled over on a 15-month lead, PMI prices follow.
items.angle: Gives a falsifiable dashboard for the Dec hike debate: 2y 4.65% / 4.45% and the January odds repricing (35% -> 50%).
items.tweetA: Brent -6%, 2y +5bp. When oil can't pull yields down, the market is telling you the Fed is the marginal price-setter again. The question is whether that's inflation or politics - and the 2y vs 4.65% settles it inside two weeks.
items.tweetB: The post-midterm theory: the political irritant is gone, so the hawks quietly turn back into doves after one 'promise-keeping' hike December. If that's right, the 2027 strip is ~30bp too high. If wrong, 50bp is live. Pick a side before the 10y auction.

items.title: CTAs at -35 from +60, will sell ~$60B S&P in a flat month; vol-control sold $101B
items.idea: Tier1Alpha trend-follower index fell to ~-35 from >+60 in late October. In a flat tape the model sells ~$60B of S&P over the next month; needs a close over ~7,700 (150pts up) to turn buyer. 1m realized vol ~22 vs 3m ~15 (widest gap since April 2025), so vol-control can't re-lever ($101B sold last week). Systematic z-score -1.0. Monday's 2.35% day was covering, not new bids.
items.angle: Positioning is clean on discretionary, not on systematic. A 'quiet print' that pulls realized below 15 by Friday is the re-leveraging trigger.
items.tweetA: Monday's +2.35% was a short squeeze with a systematic hangover: CTAs still sell ~$60B in a flat tape and vol-control can't buy until realized drops under 15. The market needs boredom more than it needs good news.
items.tweetB: Strange asymmetry: S&P within 2% of its pre-crash level while the biggest mechanical buyers are still sidelined. Either the tape is strong enough to force them back above 7,700, or Monday was the high. No middle.

items.title: The factor damage: GS high-beta momentum pair -50% from high, worse than 2021
items.idea: Goldman's high-beta momentum pair is 50% off its high (2021: ~47%, 2016: 33%). iCapital: Nasdaq-100 one-day drops of 6.4%+ (Thursday's was first since 2020) -> next month avg +2.5%, positive 61%; next year avg -4.2%, median -24.4%, positive only 30%. Augur's affine model puts expected 10y US equity returns at 1.9%. McClellan reads Monday as a 'rogue wave' completing, with seasonality resuming.
items.angle: Short-term bounce / medium-term damage framing: base rates say buy the month, sell the year.
items.tweetA: Base rates after a 6.4% Nasdaq-100 day: +2.5% next month (61% hit rate), then -4.2% avg over the year with a -24% median. The bounce is real. The 30% hit rate on the year is what should keep you honest.
items.tweetB: High-beta momentum -50%, worse than 2021. Last time that factor broke this hard, the market spent a year proving it. Monday's squeeze got us back to flat versus the election - which tells you how little the squeeze fixed.

items.title: Anthropic roadshow starts today: $90.4B raise at $70-78/share, run-rate revenue ~$81B
items.idea: Draft prospectus: IPO up to $64.4B plus $26B private placements from cornerstone investors (Alphabet, Nvidia, AMD, Broadcom, Microsoft, TSMC, Micron) = $90.4B at $70-78/share. Run-rate revenue ~$81B at 31 Oct, up $10B in one month. Trading starts next Thu/Fri. Dauber: it's a bid for the same dollars that own the listed AI complex; Nvidia prints 17 Nov, 'two prices for the same demand, days apart'.
items.angle: Supply of AI paper: $90B is the largest fee event of the year and a liquidity drain on the listed AI stack the same week as NVDA earnings.
items.tweetA: $10B of run-rate revenue added in ONE MONTH. For scale, that's a Starbucks-sized business appearing between two Fridays. And the cornerstones are Nvidia, AMD, Broadcom, TSMC, Micron - the suppliers are funding their biggest customer's IPO.
items.tweetB: A $90B raise lands the same week as Nvidia earnings. The market gets two prices for the same demand - one from the supplier, one from the customer. If they disagree, guess which one the semis trade off.

items.title: SoftBank +14% on a $7B loss; 5y CDS at 466bp; $3.7B write-down on power-equipment advances
items.idea: SoftBank rallied ~14% after a quarter losing ~$7B, incl. a $3.7B charge on advance payments for US data-center power equipment after it changed procurement, financing costs more than doubled, $5B margin loan against Arm shares. 5y CDS 466bp (4-yr wide). Dauber: equity bought for Arm/OpenAI marks, protection market looks at the balance sheet; CoreWeave (CDS >1,000bp) reports tonight - same question 'with less equity underneath'.
items.angle: Two markets, two answers on the same entity. AI financing stress is in CDS, not in spreads or bank credit yet.
items.tweetA: SoftBank: stock +14%, CDS 466bp. The equity market is buying the Arm stake; the credit market is reading the balance sheet. One of them is going to have to apologize - CoreWeave tonight is the next test of who.
items.tweetB: A $3.7B write-down on advance payments for power equipment is what a cancelled data center looks like on a balance sheet. It's the first hard number I've seen on the 'we ordered more than we can use' risk. Watch who else prepaid.

items.title: Consumer credit: charge-offs falling, delinquencies rising, 14% expect to miss a payment
items.idea: Synchrony master-trust net charge-offs 3.86% (from 4.19%), Capital One card 3.98% (from 4.63% YoY) - but Synchrony 30-day delinquency 1.9% (from 1.78%), seven-issuer avg 2.6% from 2.51%, Affirm 30d 2.9% (+35bp). Delinquency leads loss by ~2 quarters. NY Fed: probability of missing a minimum payment ~14%, only reached in 2020 spike and 2024-25 peaks. BofA data: trade-down to value merchants.
items.angle: Lead vs lag: the number on the wall (charge-offs) is the lagging one. A hike into rising delinquencies is a funding-cost event for lenders, a fee event for networks.
items.tweetA: Card charge-offs are falling. Delinquencies are rising. One of those leads the other by two quarters. I'd position for the leading one and let the lagging one catch up.
items.tweetB: Networks collect on nominal spending and carry no loan. Lenders carry both. A December hike into a 14% 'might miss a payment' consumer is the clearest V vs COF/SYF divergence setup I've seen this year. $V $MA $COF $SYF

items.title: Banks: a hike through a flattening curve - money centers over regionals
items.idea: 2s10s flattened to 32bp from 38bp (28 Oct), the 2-year carrying the whole move. Money centers beat regionals Monday: GS +4.67% $906, C +2.48%, BAC +2.29%, JPM +2.27%. KRE +14.5% YTD vs XLF +6.9%. BAC sits 22.5% below its 52w high with 50dma under 200dma. CME October ADV record 30M contracts (rates +28%, Treasuries +48%). Anthropic raise = largest fee event of the year; equity underwriting revenue down 19% this quarter. Berkshire is buying Class A from holders and retiring them.
items.angle: Curve slope, not level, is what regionals haven't been given. Exchanges/underwriters get paid by uncertainty.
items.tweetA: Regionals already won the 'higher rates' trade on level. Slope is what they haven't been paid for - and 2s10s at 32bp says they won't be. $KRE $JPM $CME
items.tweetB: Uncertainty has a P&L: CME did a record 30M contracts a day in October and Treasury contracts jumped 48%. A December meeting priced at 96% rather than 100% is a hedging event every day until the 9th. Own the toll booth.

items.title: China October imports +41.6%, exports +35.2%; Kospi record 5,239; Nikkei 60,459
items.idea: China's October exports +35.2% and imports +41.6% (fastest import growth in five years); surplus >$1.04T YTD though October's $105.3B missed $126.5B. Kospi +4.39% to record 5,239, Nikkei +2.87% to 60,459.58 on chips. Infineon guides FY27 to ~EUR20B. BoJ October summary debated faster hikes with yen at 158. Also: Abu Dhabi trilateral US-Russia-Ukraine talks opened (first since Feb); Russia reimposed fuel rationing (30L cities, 50L highways) after drones hit >=8 refineries; France blames IRGC for cyberattacks shutting refrigeration at ~700 supermarkets.
items.angle: Imports +41.6% is a restocking/AI-capex signal as much as demand. Russian domestic fuel rationing is a real constraint on the war economy.
items.tweetA: China imports +41.6% - fastest in five years - in a month the world was told demand was fading. Add Korea at a record on memory and the data says the AI hardware cycle isn't in Asia's numbers as a bubble, it's in them as a shortage.
items.tweetB: Russia is rationing fuel (30L per fill in cities) after drones hit eight refineries - on the same morning delegations sit down in Abu Dhabi. Leverage at the table is increasingly measured in refinery throughput.

items.title: Take-Two: guide 6% below street, stock +4% after hours on 'GTA VI is ten days away'
items.idea: Bookings $1.6B vs $1.65B expected; held FY guide $8.0-8.2B vs street $8.6B; stock closed $207.40 (-3.5%) then $215.72 after hours when management said GTA VI is 'ten days away' with pre-orders at 'unprecedented levels' and no number. Dauber's 'shadow traded as the thing'. Also a one-line aside: 'Cybertruck, we hardly knew ya!'
items.angle: Guide-vs-adjective: when the product date is the only variable the guide is noise.
items.tweetA: Take-Two guided 6% below the street and the stock rallied 4% on an adjective. When a single launch date is the whole thesis, the guide is decoration. $TTWO
items.tweetB: 'Pre-orders at unprecedented levels' with no number is the tell: if it were record-breaking in a quantifiable way they'd print it. Doesn't mean it's bad - means the market is paying for a feeling.

items.title: HY 342bp (5th obs over 325), CCC 1,317bp; BDC marks split; Blackstone Secured Lending cut
items.idea: High yield printed 342bp for 6 Nov (6bp tighter, 5th observation over the 325 line), IG 93bp, CCC 1,317bp. BDC marks split: Blue Owl NAV +6c with non-accruals 0.8% vs New Mountain NAV -22c, non-accruals 1.8%. A second dividend cut after Blackstone Secured Lending 'turns the group'. Levels to watch: HY 355bp (credit leads equities lower) / 326bp (contained).
items.angle: The AI build stress is in single names (SB, CRWV), not yet in index credit - which is the window.
items.tweetA: HY at 342 is not stress. SoftBank at 466 and CoreWeave north of 1,000 is stress. The index is hiding the problem inside a handful of AI-financed names. 355bp is where the index stops hiding it.
items.tweetB: Blue Owl NAV +6c, New Mountain -22c. Private credit isn't a single trade anymore - it's a dispersion trade. A second BDC dividend cut is the signal I'd wait for before calling it systemic. $OWL $BXSL

items.title: Waller leads, Warsh disagrees: forward guidance split before CPI; AI buildout absent from Fed's frame
items.idea: Waller: 'September's inflation data were bad. There was no silver lining.' Supports 25bp December even if October improves; 50bp 'should be considered' if core ~0.3% again. Boockvar notes Waller never mentioned the AI trade (picks-and-shovels cut in half), rising financing costs or the uncertain pace of data-center construction - while Chair Warsh did at the last presser. Boockvar (self-declared hawk) argues the Fed has no choice but to watch the AI buildout because of its influence on labor, inflation and the stock market. Only m/o/m CPI because of the shutdown.
items.angle: Fed internal split: Warsh sees AI capex as a macro variable, Waller doesn't. That's the dovish path if equities break.
items.tweetA: The Fed has a Chair who watches the AI capex cycle and a governor who doesn't mention it. If picks-and-shovels are down 50% and data-center permits are freezing, whose model breaks first when the data softens? $SPY $NVDA
items.tweetB: Even the hawk Boockvar says it: the AI buildout is too big for the Fed to ignore. Data center capex is both an inflation source (high-tech goods, Waller says) and the thing that breaks if rates go up. The Fed is hiking into its own transmission channel.

items.title: NY Fed: unemployment-increase expectations highest since April 2020; delinquency risk 13.8%; gas under $4
items.idea: NY Fed Consumer Expectations: 1y inflation expectations held at 3.9%; expectation of higher unemployment is the highest since April 2020; job-finding expectations best since Nov 2025; probability of missing a minimum debt payment +1.6pp to 13.8% (highest since Dec 2025). Dallas Fed Banking Survey: credit standards and terms tightened, loan pricing up broadly, loan performance weakened, bankers expect a decline in business activity and deterioration in loan performance in 6 months. Gasoline fell below $4 ($3.98) for first time since mid-July (vs $3.07 a year ago).
items.angle: Households are simultaneously more afraid of job loss and more confident they could find one - labor-market 'churn fear' rather than layoffs.
items.tweetA: Expecting unemployment to rise: highest since April 2020. Expecting to find a job: highest since Nov 2025. Households are describing a low-hire, high-churn market. That's not recession, it's stagnation with a credit squeeze attached.
items.tweetB: Dallas Fed bankers tightening credit while raising loan prices and still seeing more demand. That's what a late-cycle borrower looks like: willing to pay up because the alternative is not getting funded.

items.source: David Rosenberg / Early Morning with Dave
items.title: Cheaper oil, depleted reserves: Rosenberg favors energy infrastructure/storage
items.idea: Rosenberg: declining oil prices are fueling risk-on beyond the 'TACO trade' - more oil is flowing from the Middle East, production is growing elsewhere, and households/businesses conserve. But the Iran war has drained global stockpiles to the lowest in many years, so the race is on to replenish reserves and build storage 'before the next supply shock'. Futures are fully priced for a Dec 9 hike after Waller.
items.angle: Pick-and-shovel energy: price falls but inventory restocking creates a floor; infrastructure/storage is the volume trade, not the price trade.
items.tweetA: Oil down 6% and everyone calls it a peace dividend. Inventories are at multi-year lows. The restock bid means every dip is a refill order - storage and midstream own the volume whichever way crude goes.
items.tweetB: If you were the Strategic Reserve or a utility, would you rather buy storage at $85 or hope for $70? The mere existence of the war premium is also forcing a build-out of tankage and pipelines. Infrastructure is the Iran-war trade that doesn't need Brent.

items.source: Stephen Innes / Dark Side of the Boom (CPI)
items.title: Goldman's 0.16% core vs 0.22% consensus: shutdown seasonal distortion + health insurance reset
items.idea: Goldman (Rindels/Walker) expects Oct core CPI of 0.16% vs unrounded consensus ~0.22%; JPM and DB less dovish. Rates market prices ~86% of a Dec hike. Missing 2025 shutdown data distort this month's seasonals, health insurance undergoes a statistical reset, and a soft CPI may not translate to benign PCE. Innes calls out the irony of trading the 2nd decimal with no annual comparison.
items.angle: Dispersion of bank forecasts is itself a trade: a 0.16 and a 0.30 are different Fed paths.
items.tweetA: Goldman is at 0.16% core when the Street is at 0.22 and ING is at 0.30. A 14bp spread between forecasters on the single most important print of the month, on a data set with a shutdown hole in the seasonals. This is when you size smaller, not bigger.
items.tweetB: Everyone is arguing about whether CPI is hot or cool. The more important question is whether the seasonal adjustment even works this month. If Goldman is right about the distortion, 'cool' is a statistical artifact and the Fed will know it.

items.source: Stephen Innes / Dark Side of the Boom (FX Daily)
items.title: Gold's 'correlation paralysis': oil down, equities up, dollar down - and gold flat
items.idea: Gold is failing to respond to falling crude, recovering equities and a weaker dollar: it's waiting for CPI. ING sees core +0.3% m/m (above 0.2% consensus). The Fed's target is consistent with ~0.17% monthly. ~20bp of Dec tightening priced. EUR/USD sits ~1.5-1.7% below rate-differential fair value, 1.1200-1.1250 range, 1.1300 into year-end if French risk premium eases. Bowman/Waller/Logan/Schmid all speak today. Nvidia fell 4% yet S&P/Nasdaq within 2% of their Nov 4 closes.
items.angle: Gold at $4,085 has been trading like liquidity-sensitive risk or inverse oil on different days; the dominant driver is about to be re-selected by the 2y.
items.tweetA: Gold didn't rally on lower oil, a weaker dollar and a bid for risk. Three 'good for gold' signals and nothing. When a market ignores bullish signals ahead of a catalyst, it's telling you which signal it actually believes.
items.tweetB: Gold at $4,085 trading like a liquidity asset on Tuesdays and an inflation hedge on Wednesdays is a sign nobody owns it for a reason. A real-yield breakdown after CPI would tell you which regime we're in. $GLD

items.source: Stephen Innes / Dark Side of the Boom (Goldman)
items.title: Goldman GOAL Kickstart: AI trade is rotating, semis decoupling from hyperscalers - not turning defensive
items.idea: Goldman's Mueller-Glissmann team stays constructive: positioning has improved, valuations are more attractive, earnings supportive; the AI trade is going through a significant rotation, semis breaking from the hyperscalers financing them, volatility at intensity not seen since the pandemic, a Democratic sweep adds political uncertainty on AI infrastructure. Cross-asset risk indicators constructive but one threshold remains distant. (Body paywalled after intro; summary only.)
items.angle: Semis vs hyperscaler spread as the new AI factor: suppliers rebound while the spenders get questioned.
items.tweetA: Semis +6.85% Monday, with Nvidia the only decliner. Goldman says the AI trade is rotating, not ending - from the spenders to the suppliers. That's the opposite of the 2024-25 trade, where hyperscaler capex was the asset.
items.tweetB: A Democratic sweep adds a new layer: committee subpoena power over Big Tech and AI infrastructure. Goldman isn't ready to abandon the bull market - but nobody has priced Warren chairing Banking and Coons chairing SFRC.

items.source: Stephen Innes / Dark Side of the Boom (BTIG)
items.title: BTIG: first 80% downside-volume NYSE session in nearly a year; Nasdaq below 200dma; fat pitch not yet
items.idea: BTIG's Jonathan Krinsky: last Thursday delivered the correlation-driven liquidation he wanted (Nasdaq broke decisively below its 200-day; NYSE's first 80% downside-volume session in nearly a year), but one ugly session rarely finishes the job. His historical washout work puts the preferred buy lower; investors trapped above in semis are the supply; defensive hideouts look vulnerable; conflicting bottoming indicators. (Intro only; rest paywalled.)
items.angle: Bounce vs durable bottom: oversold isn't washed out. Trapped longs in semis = overhead supply.
items.tweetA: 80% downside volume is a capitulation signal. But Krinsky's point is that one day rarely finishes a bottom - and half the semis complex is full of people waiting to get out at breakeven. Supply overhead beats oversold.
items.tweetB: Wild: the market is within 2% of its pre-crash close and BTIG is still waiting for a 'fat pitch'. That's the disconnect - tape says V-bottom, technicians say second leg. Position size matters more than direction here.

items.title: Permit vs power: Santa Clara upgrades 2028-30, Spartanburg developer renegotiating power date after 12-month pause proposal
items.idea: After the midterms, opposition to new data centers gained momentum, esp. Texas. Santa Clara had 13 data centers approved/under construction in 2023 but grid upgrades won't arrive until 2028-2030. In Spartanburg, SC, a developer who paid $4M for a utility commitment of 60 MW by Sept 2026 began discussing a later power-delivery date when the county proposed a 12-month pause on approvals. AI selloff reflects fear that approvals tighten beyond existing power constraints.
items.angle: Is the AI buildout power-limited or permit-limited? The answer varies by county - which makes 'GW announced' a worse metric than 'GW energized'.
items.tweetA: Santa Clara approved 13 data centers in 2023 and the grid upgrade that powers them arrives in 2028-30. The AI buildout isn't capex-constrained - it's electrons and county commissioners. 'GW announced' is a vanity metric.
items.tweetB: Spartanburg: developer paid $4M for 60 MW by Sept 2026, then the county floated a 12-month pause and the power date started to slip. Local politics reaches into utility contracts. Post-midterm permitting is a new AI risk factor.

items.title: 800 VDC: 600kW-1MW racks vs 200-250kW today; first commercial SST deployment in China (Envision, 10kV->800V)
items.idea: Rack power moves from 48-54VDC to 800VDC: enables 600kW-1MW racks vs ~200-250kW today, lowers resistive losses, removes conversion stages. Staged adoption: near term rack 'sidecars', medium term row-level DC busways, long term solid-state transformers (10kV MV AC directly to 800VDC). Envision announced the world's first commercial 800V DC system at its Galaxy AI campus in Ulanqab, China. Limit: removing 600kW-1MW heat per rack needs advanced liquid cooling; Kyber (144 GPUs/rack) reportedly delayed by copper midplane issues; Nvidia's NVL576 links eight Oberon NVL72 racks via optical/copper.
items.angle: China is first to commercial SST + 800VDC; the power-semis/SST supply chain is the beneficiary if US permitting slows density-first.
items.tweetA: The first commercial 800VDC AI campus is in Ulanqab, China - not Texas. If permits constrain footprints in the US, power density becomes the only lever, and SST/power-semi suppliers are a pure play on that. Watch who has the gear.
items.tweetB: Kyber's copper midplane delay means optics (spread across racks) and densification (more watts/rack) are both blocked from different ends. Whoever solves the 1MW rack first sets the next Nvidia cadence.

items.title: More tokens per watt: OpenAI 'Jalapeño' 1.5-1.9x throughput/watt vs Nvidia; AMD bought Taalas HC1
items.idea: OpenAI's Jalapeño inference accelerator reports 1.5-1.9x higher inference throughput per watt than the NVIDIA systems tested across three public models (early, company-reported). d-Matrix and Qualcomm go memory-centric. Taalas HC1 (bought by AMD) hard-wires a model into silicon to eliminate memory movement - radical specialization when power is scarce. Edge inference is 'the holy grail' but useful results at the edge have been hard so far.
items.angle: OpenAI building its own chip and AMD buying Taalas: the Nvidia-margin story now has 3 vendors attacking tokens/watt.
items.tweetA: OpenAI says its own inference chip does 1.5-1.9x the throughput per watt of Nvidia. Company-reported, early, three models. But when power is the binding constraint, a 50% efficiency gain is worth more than a 50% discount. $NVDA $AMD
items.tweetB: AMD buying Taalas - a company that bakes a model into silicon - is the most underrated move in the AI hardware story this month. If model churn slows, hard-wired inference eats general-purpose GPUs from below.

items.source: Michael Spencer & Joachim Klement / AI Supremacy
items.title: Klement: SLMs match LLMs in 81.2% of tasks at 50-85% lower energy; 7x inference-per-watt; 'hyperscalers are toast'
items.idea: Stanford research (May) compared SLMs (Qwen 3, Gemma 3, GPT-OSS, Granite 4.0) on local PCs vs ChatGPT 5 / Claude Sonnet 4.5 / Gemini 2.5 Pro: win-or-tie 98.6% on chat, 62.5% on reasoning, 81.2% task-weighted. SLM reasoning success on hardest level 5: 51.5%. SLMs have 50-85% lower compute/energy costs and ~7x inference/watt. Estimated US addressable SLM market ~$10tn (one-third of GDP). Klement: AI bubble bursts 2027 or 2028; S&P to ~5,000 by end-2027 (-33% from ~7,500). Agentic tasks still <50% for SLMs.
items.angle: If 70-80% of tasks move to device, hyperscaler capex ROI is mis-sized. Winners: Dell/Apple. Counter: agentic and level-5 reasoning still need clouds.
items.tweetA: 98.6% win-or-tie for small models on chat; 81% task-weighted. If that's right, the question isn't 'is AI overbuilt' - it's 'which 20% of tasks justify $1T of data centers'. I'd want to see that revenue number before I own the capex.
items.tweetB: Klement's S&P 5,000 call is a 33% drawdown from here - and relies on mean reversion more than on SLMs. The SLM thesis is the catalyst, the valuation is the fuel. Different risk from 'AI doesn't work'.

charts.desc: Four win/tie-ratio charts: SLM vs LLM across chat (98.6%), reasoning (62.5%), blended (81.2%), and by difficulty level 2023->Oct 2025

items.source: Michael Spencer & Joachim Klement / AI Supremacy
items.title: Fable/Mythos 5.2: 2.5x fast mode, 30% faster; 'Anthropic will have to IPO significantly lower than anticipated'
items.idea: Michael Spencer notes Claude Mythos / Fable 5.2 launched with an optional fast mode speeding generation up to 2.5x and 30% faster default output, the first 'frontier' release since execs called for slowdown ('We called for pacing, not pausing' - Dianne Penn). He argues autonomous engineering improved cadence and the model admits what it doesn't know. He also writes Anthropic 'will have to IPO significantly lower than previously anticipated' - at odds with Dauber's $70-78 / $81B run-rate prospectus numbers.
items.angle: Cadence speed is the moat; hallucination-admitting is an enterprise-adoption unlock.
items.tweetA: 'Admits when it doesn't know' is a bigger commercial feature than 30% faster. Enterprise adoption has been gated by confident wrong answers, not tokens/sec. $81B run-rate says the market's already voting.
items.tweetB: One newsletter says Anthropic must IPO lower than expected; another has the draft at $70-78/share with $81B run-rate up $10B in a month. Both can't be true. Thursday-Friday finds out.

items.title: Equal-weight S&P outperformed, breadth >5:1, market roughly unchanged from pre-election
items.idea: Marsh: Monday equal-weight S&P beat cap-weight because Nvidia (2nd-largest S&P weight) fell >4%; advancers outnumbered decliners >5:1. After all the commotion, the market is roughly unchanged from before the election.
items.angle: NVDA concentration as a breadth-measurement artifact.
items.tweetA: 5:1 advance/decline and the cap-weighted index lags because one stock - the second-biggest weight - fell 4% on a personal scandal. That's the real concentration risk: index-level idiosyncratic tail risk on a single name.
items.tweetB: The market is back to pre-election levels after a violent crash and a squeeze. Net result of the whole circus: zero. Which is exactly why the vol is the story, not the level.

items.title: Trade Desk +23% AH: Q3 revenue $736M vs $651M; but ex-partner deal rev -3.5%; Q4 guide >=$755M vs $690M
items.idea: TTD Q3 rev $736M (-0.5% YoY) vs consensus $651M; adj. EBITDA $266M vs ~$160M guide; Q4 guide >= $755M vs ~$685-695M. But ~3pts of growth came from a non-recurring strategic-partner transaction (ex that -3.5%) plus mid-single-digit % political ads. Sept 15% layoff -> >$100M gross 2027 savings. Netflix Kokai integration live Nov; Koa improved median CPA 21% across 62 campaigns; JBP +30%. $731M added to buyback ($1B total). Stock $14.93 close, $18.32 AH.
items.angle: A beat quality question: political + one-off partner revenue flatter the print.
items.tweetA: TTD beat revenue by 13% and the stock rips 23% after hours - to a price where ex-one-offs revenue is still shrinking 3.5% year over year. A turnaround, or a short squeeze with a nice deck? $TTD
items.tweetB: Watch the sequential: management says no normal Q4 seasonal lift, politics fades in 2027. The beat is real, the base is distorted. A $1B buyback at $14 is the market's real vote.

items.title: Samsung/Google AI glasses with Warby Parker: preorders Nov 12, delivery mid-Dec, up to 1pt of 2027 growth
items.idea: WRBY +18.6% on reports the Samsung/Google (Gemini, Android XR) glasses designed with Warby Parker and Gentle Monster open for preorder Nov 12, ahead of December launch. Initial devices: audio+camera, no in-lens display. Demos in 65 of 364 stores; guidance includes up to 1pp revenue growth from Intelligent Eyewear, recognized on delivery. UBS 2027 rev est $1.255B (+$104M for glasses). Q3 revenue +10.4% to $244.7M, gross margin 54.4%.
items.angle: Retail distribution of AI wearables: prescription fulfillment + store footprint as the actual moat.
items.tweetA: The AI glasses hardware is Samsung and the model is Google. The distribution moat is a 364-store optician network with prescription labs. Meta has the Ray-Ban deal; Google went to the other eyewear incumbent. $WRBY
items.tweetB: 'Up to 1 point' of revenue growth from AI glasses in 2027 is the number to anchor on. A stock +22% on that is pricing preorder surprise, not guidance. Nov 12 preorders are the first read on whether anyone wants a camera on their face.

items.title: AI rebound is hardware: AMD +13% (Oppenheimer upgrade), Coherent +16.8% on optics, KLA +9.3% on advanced packaging
items.idea: AMD +13.26% to $508.58 on Oppenheimer upgrade (server/data-center share gains, favorable pricing as incumbent supplier in next-gen deals); Coherent +16.79% to $225.19 with Lumentum on optical demand; KLA +9.31% to $151.38 on advanced packaging metrology. Hims & Hers -11.8% (revenue miss, guide cut, GLP-1 transition); Monday.com -9.1% on downgrades (weaker upmarket sales, higher small-customer churn).
items.angle: Software loses (MNDY, HIMS), hardware wins - AI winner/loser split continues on a bounce day.
items.tweetA: Monday's rebound was hardware. AMD, Coherent, KLA up 9-17%; the software names with 'AI transition' headwinds (monday.com) fell on downgrades. The market isn't buying 'AI' - it's buying the physical layer and selling the seat-based software. $COHR $KLAC $MNDY
items.tweetB: AMD at $508 after an upgrade citing 'favorable pricing as an incumbent'. That sentence would have been absurd 18 months ago. The data-center share story has quietly become a pricing-power story.

items.title: Best day of the year: all S&P sectors green, 84% of stocks advanced; uranium, memory, miners, airlines led
items.idea: Macro Charts: Monday all S&P sectors were green and 84% of the S&P advanced - the most since November 2025. Leaders: uranium, memory, miners, airlines, semis, precious metals. 'Yesterday was the opposite of what consensus expected. Opinions are expensive… focus on price.' Offers an 'actionable execution plan' (paywalled) with a 'clear window to respond'.
items.angle: Breadth thrust after a crash is a different signal than a bounce; leaders were the most beaten-up cyclicals.
items.tweetA: 84% of S&P stocks up in a day - the most in a year - and the leaders were uranium, memory and airlines. That's not a rotation into quality. That's a violent unwind of the shorts in everything that got hit.
items.tweetB: Airlines and memory in the same top-five list is a fascinating combination: lower oil and AI hardware. One macro driver (cheaper energy) and one thematic (AI shortage) both squeezing at once. Hard to keep both.

items.title: Frankopan on the Nvidia affair: ~$200B wiped from NVDA in a day
items.idea: Frankopan argues Jensen Huang 'is no ordinary corporate executive', sitting at the intersection of US AI supremacy and the US-China rivalry; ~$200B of Nvidia's market cap was wiped yesterday on the exposé. He promises a fuller geopolitical read (the visible email is an intro; remainder paywalled/linked) and a new weekend round-up format.
items.angle: The tail risk was personal and political, not technical - China didn't need a rare-earth ban to dent Nvidia.
items.tweetA: ~$200B of market value gone in a day over a personnel scandal. Not a demand miss, not export controls, not a competitor. The most valuable company in the world has a key-person and counterintelligence risk nobody was modelling. $NVDA
items.tweetB: AI bubble bears spent three years waiting for a demand air pocket. The catalyst was a counterintelligence story. Lesson: concentration risk in a single CEO is its own factor.

items.title: Commerce stopped enforcing Biden-era chip license rule in May 2025; $80B of AI chips to SG/MY/TH this year
items.idea: McGuire (CFR): the consequential decision wasn't H200s to China - it was May 2025, when the Trump administration stopped enforcing the Biden rule requiring licenses for large AI-chip orders to non-trusted companies in most countries, promised a replacement and never delivered. The #2, #4 and #5 importers of AI chips this year are Singapore, Malaysia and Thailand: $80B in aggregate. He calls it the largest tech transfer of controlled goods to an adversary in history.
items.angle: Third-country transshipment is a bigger volume channel than direct China sales; the NVDA China revenue line understates exposure.
items.tweetA: Singapore, Malaysia and Thailand imported $80B of AI chips this year. Combined GDP of the three doesn't absorb that. The Nvidia 'China is zero' narrative has a very large footnote.
items.tweetB: The Biden license rule wasn't repealed, it was just not enforced - and no replacement came. That's the most important regulatory arbitrage in semis: policy on paper, policy-free in practice. A lame-duck NDAA could change that overnight.

items.title: Megaspeed: $4.8B of chips shipped while Commerce sat on intelligence; Kessler discussed investigation with Nvidia
items.idea: Megaspeed (Singapore cloud co.) is suspected of smuggling Nvidia chips to China; an executive was allegedly working for MSS. McGuire: Commerce sat on information that Megaspeed was run by Chinese spies while $4.8B in chips shipped; NYT reports BIS Under Secretary Kessler discussed Commerce's investigation with Nvidia; Commerce probe was taken over by DOJ. Megaspeed still buys chips today and is still listed as an official Nvidia cloud partner. Most chips came via Aivres, the US subsidiary of entity-listed Inspur.
items.angle: Enforcement vs. policy: legal channel to Chinese buyers inside the US (Aivres/Inspur) is a loophole that can be closed by rule.
items.tweetA: A US subsidiary of an entity-listed Chinese company can legally buy Nvidia chips inside the US. That's the loophole. Congress doesn't need a new law for it - Commerce does. The question is why Commerce hasn't.
items.tweetB: $4.8B shipped while the government 'knew'. Either that's a failure of coordination or a decision. McGuire says 'not warning Jensen was a choice'. The market has priced a CEO scandal. It hasn't priced a congressional investigation of Commerce.

items.title: Lame-duck chip bills: MATCH (DUV), RASA (remote access), OVERWATCH (no Blackwells to China) - likely via NDAA
items.idea: McGuire: the Nvidia affair makes MATCH (cuts off DUV, forces SME controls), RASA (Remote Access Security Act) and OVERWATCH (no Blackwells to China) more likely; probably attached to the NDAA, though NDAA status is uncertain post-election. Warren is incoming Banking chair, Coons incoming SFRC chair. Commerce could impose global license requirements for large orders, remote-access limits and ban Chinese companies buying chips in the US - 'only place in the world Chinese companies are legally allowed to buy chips is inside the US'.
items.angle: ASML/AMAT/LRCX/KLAC exposure to MATCH; hyperscaler remote-access.
items.tweetA: MATCH cuts off DUV. That's ASML, and the entire installed-base servicing revenue in China. The Nvidia scandal just handed a bipartisan bill the momentum it lacked. $ASML $AMAT $LRCX
items.tweetB: RASA targets cloud access: rent compute from a US-listed hyperscaler and you can sidestep chip controls. That's a direct hit to the remote-access leg of every neo-cloud's Chinese customer base.

items.title: Cantor Fitzgerald's #3 exposure is Nvidia; 'My kids now run my business' - conflicts in export policy
items.idea: McGuire: per SEC filings, Cantor Fitzgerald's third-largest exposure (and 3rd-largest unhedged) is Nvidia stock, behind S&P 500 and Amazon; bigger total exposures are AMD and Marvell. Lutnick's former firm is heavily indexed on semis while Commerce adopts policies preferential to one company. Schneider cites Witkoff's quote: 'I'm not conflicted. My kids now run my business.' Also: DOJ alleging Saudi government involvement in a plot to spy on OpenAI; Schneider on Nvidia lobbying donations to the ballroom/presidential library.
items.angle: Political-risk lens on chip policy: conflict-of-interest narrative will fuel Democratic oversight in January.
items.tweetA: Cantor's third-largest exposure is Nvidia, and the Commerce Secretary's old firm is running chip policy. You don't need to believe anything sinister - you only need to know Warren and Coons will say it out loud in January. $NVDA
items.tweetB: DOJ alleges Saudi involvement in a plot to spy on OpenAI. Nvidia has a spy story. These are the same story: frontier AI is now treated as a state target. Security spend is going to be a standard AI capex line.

items.title: A brief history of honey traps: Jael, Romeos, and the CIA parking a compromised officer at the Hoover Institution
items.idea: Schneider's tongue-in-cheek tour: Jael of Judges 4 (tent peg), Cold War 'Romeo' agents, a 1950s UK case of drugged/photographed Soviet naval attaché blackmailed for a decade, a CIA-compromised officer given a job at the Hoover Institution rather than jailed, Mossad's 1986 Italy operation, Okhrana-era deep-cover programs, and The Illegals (Shaun Walker, 2025). Also notes Nazi-era brothels in France/Poland deliberately infected officers.
items.angle: Pattern: access to individuals who control scarce resources is the oldest intelligence play; now the scarce resource is compute allocation.
items.tweetA: Honeypots work on whoever allocates scarce things. In 1950 it was a naval attaché. In 2026 it's whoever decides who gets Blackwells. The nature of the resource changed. The attack didn't.
items.tweetB: 'Access to Jensen means access to more compute.' Compute allocation is now a strategic gate, and gates attract exactly the sort of people who manipulate gatekeepers. Expect Chinese and Gulf actors to treat chip allocators like oil ministers.

items.title: Vitalik: ETH's value is 'stability', not fee burn; burn offset only ~2% of issuance in 2026
items.idea: Buterin: 'We should not feel sad if fee burn is less than 10% of breakeven indefinitely' - ETH's value comes from decentralization, censorship resistance and security. Through 9M 2026 the burn offset ~2% of issuance while supply grew 0.64%. He warns that chasing fee revenue means wanting congestion, turning Ethereum into 'a world-scale major corporation'. Tom Lee calls it 'a seismic shift'; Ethlabs argues ETH beats BTC on quantum and AI risk and EF holds <0.2% of supply. Morning Minute: store-of-value is Bitcoin's category (hard cap, Lindy, ETF plumbing, treasury bid), and Zcash is creeping in as privacy SoV.
items.angle: ETH narrative pivot from yield/burn to monetary premium - competing directly with BTC for the same bid.
items.tweetA: ETH is now a 'store of value' with a 0.64% annual supply growth, 2% burn offset, and ETF outflows of $185M a day. Bitcoin's pitch needed a hard cap and it still can't hold $75k. Good luck with this pivot.
items.tweetB: Vitalik told holders to stop valuing ETH like a cash-flow asset. BitMine owns 4.97% of supply on exactly that premise. The treasury-company model needed the fee-burn thesis less than it needs a SoV thesis - and it just got one. $ETH $BMNR

items.title: 14 public companies sold 108,247 BTC ($8.08B) in 2026; MARA + Riot = 56%
items.idea: Lookonchain: 14 public companies sold ~108,247 BTC worth $8.08B so far in 2026, with MARA at 40,581 BTC and Riot 20,264 accounting for 56%. Strategy meanwhile bought 1,036 BTC ($81.9M, avg $79,012) funded by $283.8M MSTR sale and repurchased $188.3M STRC preferred. BTC ETFs saw $201M outflows Monday (>$2B over 7 sessions); ETH ETFs -$185M. BTC $74.2k, lowest since August. Elsewhere: Strategy at $79k avg buy vs spot $74.2k - underwater on the latest tranche.
items.angle: Miners are structural sellers; treasuries are marginal buyers funded by equity issuance - and equity issuance needs a premium to NAV.
items.tweetA: Strategy bought 1,036 BTC at $79k and spent more ($188M) buying back its own preferred than it spent on Bitcoin ($82M). It's funding both with common stock. That's not accumulation, it's balance-sheet maintenance. $MSTR
items.tweetB: Public companies have sold 108k BTC this year. The ETF flows grab headlines but miners selling 61k coins is the other side of the book. 'Corporate treasury bid' is a two-way street.

items.title: IBIT in-kind redemption demand at record highs: $3.6B of self-custody BTC swapped into ETF shares
items.idea: BlackRock says demand from large holders converting self-custodied bitcoin into IBIT shares is 'the highest we've seen at any point', citing security concerns; ~ $3.6B of such in-kind swaps since the SEC permitted them. Same day: Coinbase got final OCC approval for a national trust bank charter (joining Circle in July and Ripple in October), and Binance stopped processing MEXC after FinCEN named it a primary money laundering concern. Elliptic: North Korea's TraderTraitor launders Binance hack proceeds via ~$90 meme coins on NEAR.
items.angle: Self-custody -> ETF wrapper is a security-driven flow (hacks, wrench attacks, quantum, key risk) - structurally bullish for custodians, ironically bearish for the 'be your own bank' meme.
items.tweetA: Whales are moving BTC OUT of self-custody INTO an ETF wrapper at record pace. $3.6B of 'not your keys' voluntarily. After 15 years of 'be your own bank', the largest holders voted for BlackRock. $IBIT $COIN
items.tweetB: OCC charter for Coinbase, FinCEN naming MEXC, DPRK laundering through $90 meme coins. Everything in crypto is converging on a federally-supervised perimeter. The wild west gets walled in from both sides.

items.title: Trump 'knows nothing' about World Liberty; Warren will make Trump-family crypto a first oversight target
items.idea: In a 60 Minutes interview recorded Nov 6, Trump confirmed he co-owns World Liberty Financial but knows 'nothing about it', said 'my sons run the company', and that presidents have faced this 'going back to George Washington', citing oil. It was his first sit-down after Republicans lost both chambers Nov 3. Warren, incoming Banking chair in January, will target Trump-family crypto, Big Tech CEOs, Wall Street execs and prediction markets ('Wild West-style lack of oversight'). Blumenthal gave Binance, Tether, WLF and Fight Fight Fight until Jan 4, 2027 to produce records.
items.angle: Crypto regulatory regime flips from tailwind to oversight in Jan: subpoenas to WLF/Binance/Tether; prediction markets in scope.
items.tweetA: Jan 4, 2027: records due from Binance, Tether, World Liberty, and Fight Fight Fight. Jan: Warren takes the gavel at Banking. The crypto 'pro-regulation' trade has a 60-day shelf life before it turns into a subpoena trade. $COIN $CRCL
items.tweetB: Trump says his sons run WLF and he knows nothing. In the same cycle, Warren says prediction markets are a Wild West. The industry spent 2025 buying access; it's about to find out what that access is worth under divided government.

items.title: NYSE's tokenized-stock venue picks Avalanche; Formation to run Solana venue; Schwab and PNC add on-ramps
items.idea: Ava Labs says Avalanche will be the ledger for the clearing firm behind NYSE's planned tokenized securities ATS (24/7 trading, clearing, settlement; pending approval; no date). Dennis Lee: ledger needs 'speed, operator control over participants, steady costs and a big developer base'. Formation Securities plans a Solana venue (Orca AMM; Galaxy, Exodus, Forward Industries shares) under SEC's Innovation Exemption in early 2027. Schwab adds SOL, AVAX, LINK (0.75% fee, ex-NY/LA). PNC pilots USDC acceptance for corporate clients via Coinbase. Coinbase Wallet building a web terminal, with AI agents by year-end.
items.angle: Tokenized equities are choosing chains on operator control - not decentralization. Different L1s for different venues -> fragmentation, with NYSE 'on a range of blockchains'.
items.tweetA: NYSE picked its chain on 'operator control over participants'. That's the opposite of why anyone loved a public blockchain. Tokenized equities will be real - and permissioned in all but name. $AVAX $SOL
items.tweetB: Schwab adding SOL, AVAX and LINK with a 0.75% fee, PNC accepting USDC, NYSE on Avalanche, Formation on Solana. The retail, bank, exchange and clearing rails are going on-chain in the same quarter - and BTC is at a 3-month low. The infrastructure trade has decoupled from the price.

items.title: MARA sold 13,597 BTC for $1.1B to repay $750M BTC-backed loans; Trump Media Q3 profit $409.7M is a $378M BTC gain
items.idea: MARA posted $632.1M Q3 net income on bitcoin gains, then sold 13,597 BTC (~$1.1B) to repay $750M of BTC-backed loans and approved a $500M buyback. Trump Media swung to $409.7M profit driven by gains on 15,649 BTC; ex $378.1M digital-asset gain, operations lost $23.6M. Securitize lost $66.3M on $18.6M revenue (first public quarter), buying River One. Sharplink reported $751.4M net income on $676.7M unrealized ETH gains; holds ~895k ETH. Strive buying 29 BTC/week (from 6,182 two weeks prior).
items.angle: 'Profit' in crypto treasuries is mark-to-market; real operations still lose money. Strive's weekly buys shrinking 6,182 -> 124 -> 29 is the demand curve.
items.tweetA: Trump Media: $409.7M profit, of which $378M was a BTC mark. Operations lost $23.6M. Strive's weekly purchases: 6,182 -> 124 -> 29 BTC. Treasury company demand has fallen off a cliff and the earnings are marks. $DJT
items.tweetB: MARA sold 13.6k BTC to repay loans backed by BTC. If you borrow against the asset and sell it to repay, you've just created the pro-cyclical loop the 2022 miners lived through. $MARA

items.title: Single-stock perps: Coinbase, Kalshi, Jump back CFTC; Solana's Anza proposes retiring durable nonces (Drift $295.7M exploit)
items.idea: Coinbase, Kalshi, Payward, DRW, Jump Trading and Paradigm filed an amicus brief supporting the CFTC after the Capital Markets Alliance Association sued Nov 3, arguing single-stock perpetual futures are security-based swaps that belong under the SEC. Anza proposes retiring Solana durable nonces (central to Drift's $295.7M April exploit); mainnet activation not before May 5, 2027, giving custodians six months. Also: NY enforcement action vs Kalshi not paused by a federal appeals court.
items.angle: Jurisdictional fight over 24/7 equity perps is the same fight as tokenized equities; outcome shapes who captures retail leverage.
items.tweetA: Single-stock perps are a jurisdiction fight dressed up as a product: if they're swaps, the SEC owns them; if futures, the CFTC does. Coinbase, Kalshi and Jump are on the CFTC side. The loser loses 24/7 retail leverage on equities.
items.tweetB: Solana is proposing to kill a core transaction primitive because an exploit used it - and giving custodians six months. Protocol upgrades under security pressure are going to look more like bank regulation than like crypto.

items.title: Largest weekly cut in US fundamental L/S gross since Covid - 'We're far from done'
items.idea: Lord Fed: last week produced the largest weekly reduction in US fundamental long/short gross exposure since Covid. 'Hat tip to the bears - NVDA's downfall would be a Chinese model, just not the kind they expected.' Many managers have de-risked and 'bought breathing room', but cutting exposure doesn't mean the difficult decisions are behind. (Intro only; rest paywalled.)
items.angle: De-grossing complete for fundamentals; systematic (Dauber) still has more to sell. Different holder groups, different timelines.
items.tweetA: Biggest weekly gross cut in US fundamental L/S since Covid, and the CTAs still have ~$60B to sell. One group is done, the other isn't. That's what a market that bounces and then fails looks like.
items.tweetB: Lord Fed's line - 'NVDA's downfall would be a Chinese model, just not the kind they expected' - is the cleverest take on the week. Bears waited for DeepSeek; they got a counterintelligence scandal.

items.title: Cyan Banister: 'what's coming', not 'why now' - vibe manufacturing, re-industrialization, nanotech/biotech
items.idea: Long Journey Ventures' Banister (put her IronPort exit into SpaceX, never sold): consumer wave in 2-3 years; 'vibe manufacturing' (print one widget, scale to a million, go direct) once US-China manufacturing is sorted; seeking 'the Alibaba of the Americas'; bringing semiconductor manufacturing back to the Americas; defense (Anduril to consolidate into a prime); power generation. Cost of manufacturing and robotics 'has gone down considerably'. 'I tend to not play in the why-now space; I play in the what's coming space.' Alpha is not in hot deals.
items.angle: VC lens: infrastructure layer of the last wave -> what the infrastructure enables next. Space/robotics cost curves.
items.tweetA: Cyan Banister put her whole exit into SpaceX when the rockets were still blowing up and never sold. Her seed filter: skip 'why now', find 'what's coming'. It's the opposite of how most AI capital is being deployed this week.
items.tweetB: 'Vibe manufacturing': widget -> a million units -> direct to consumer, with the Alibaba of the Americas as the missing layer. If AI lowers design cost and robotics lowers production cost, the missing piece is sourcing and logistics. That's a venture-sized hole.
